Caplan writes:
>Samuel Knoche, a student at Fordham University, has taken me up on an old bet:

---

>I bet at even odds that 10 years from now, the fraction of American 18-24 year-olds enrolled in traditional four-year colleges will be no more than 10% (not 10 percentage-points!) lower than it is today.

---

However, we’ve slightly modified the earlier terms.
> Since the most recent data is for 2015, we are betting that when the 2025 data comes out, Samuel [Knoche] wins if the fraction of 18-to-24-years-olds enrolled in four-year colleges has fallen more than 10%.  I win if it’s fallen less.  Since the current rate is 29.9%, he wins if the rate is 26.6% or less.  If the data series is discontinued, we call off the bet and I refund his money with 3% annual interest.

---

While nearly all experts cite modest mitigating factors—such as colleges' aggressive adaptation (waiving fees, direct admissions, more financial aid), the inertia of multi-year enrollment, and the slow historical pace of change—they largely agree these efforts blunt but do not reverse the 2025 shock. The most optimistic projections favor Caplan by at most 70%, while most forecasters cluster between 18% and 45% on Caplan’s chances, with the median below 40%.

Caplan’s winning scenarios hinge on the lag in new enrollment effects, aggressive domestic recruitment offsetting international losses, and possibly a sharper-than-expected drop in the denominator of 18-24-year-olds. Some also note that reporting lags, data quirks, or resilience at elite institutions might keep the rate above the threshold, but none see these as likely to guarantee victory.
